what_its_for: Natamycin is an antifungal eye drop used to treat fungal infections of the eye, including infections of the eyelid (blepharitis), the clear tissue covering the white of the eye (conjunctivitis), and the cornea (keratitis). It works by stopping the growth of fungi that are causing your eye infection.
how_to_take: Natamycin comes as eye drops. Before using, wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water. Shake the bottle well before each use. Tilt your head back, gently pull down your lower eyelid to create a small pocket, and squeeze the prescribed number of drops into the pocket. Close your eye gently for 1 to 2 minutes and press lightly on the inner corner of your eye with your finger — this helps keep the medicine in your eye. Do not touch the dropper tip to your eye, eyelid, fingers, or any other surface, as this can contaminate the drops. If you wear contact lenses, remove them before using the drops and wait at least 15 minutes before putting them back in. Do not use contact lenses while you have an active eye infection unless your doctor says it is okay.
dosing: For most fungal eye infections, the usual starting dose is 1 drop in the affected eye every 1 to 2 hours during the first 3 to 4 days. Your doctor may then reduce the dose to 1 drop 6 to 8 times per day (roughly every 3 to 4 hours) for the next several weeks. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions, as your dose may be different depending on the type and severity of your infection. Treatment usually lasts 14 to 21 days or longer. Do not stop using the drops early even if your eye feels better, unless your doctor tells you to.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, use it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular dosing schedule. Do not use extra drops to make up for a missed dose.
storage: Store natamycin eye drops at room temperature between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). You may also store it in the refrigerator, but do not freeze it. Keep the bottle tightly closed when not in use. Keep out of reach of children. Do not use the drops after the expiration date printed on the bottle. Discard any unused portion after your treatment is complete.
what_to_avoid: Avoid touching the dropper tip to any surface, including your eye or hands, to prevent contamination. Do not wear contact lenses during an active eye infection unless specifically approved by your doctor. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery right after using the drops, as your vision may be temporarily blurry. Do not share your eye drops with anyone else. Avoid rubbing your eyes after using the drops.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you experience any of the following: worsening eye pain, redness, or irritation; increased sensitivity to light; vision changes or blurred vision that does not go away; swelling around the eye; signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, itching, or difficulty breathing; your symptoms do not improve after a few days of treatment, or if they get worse at any time. Call your doctor if you accidentally swallow any of the eye drops.
when_it_works: You may start to notice some improvement in your symptoms within a few days of starting treatment. However, fungal eye infections can take several weeks to fully clear up. It is very important to continue using all of your doses for the full length of time prescribed, even if your eye starts to feel better sooner. Stopping treatment too early can allow the infection to come back or get worse.
special_populations: Pregnant or breastfeeding women should talk to their doctor before using natamycin, as its safety during pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been fully established. Natamycin eye drops are generally not recommended for children unless directed by a doctor. Elderly patients can typically use this medication safely but should follow their doctor's instructions carefully. Always tell your doctor about all other medications, eye drops, vitamins, and supplements you are taking before starting natamycin.
